question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The workers called out / the strike because / the management acceded to / all their demands.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The workers called out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct phrasal verb here should be "called off", not "called out" — the sentence reads: "The workers called out the strike because the management acceded to all their demands."

• Rule — Phrasal verb usage: "Call off" means to cancel or stop something that was planned or in progress (e.g., call off a strike, call off a meeting). "Call out" means to summon someone into action (e.g., call out the army, call out workers on strike) or to shout something loudly.

• Since the management acceded to (agreed to) all the workers' demands, logically the workers would cancel/stop the strike, not start it. So the correct verb is "called off": "The workers called off the strike because the management acceded to all their demands."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the strike because" is grammatically and logically correct as part of the sentence; no error here.

• Option 2: "all their demands" is correctly used; "their" agrees in number with "the workers" (plural), and "demands" is the appropriate plural noun.

• Option 3: "the management acceded to" is correct; "acceded to" (agreed to) is the right verb-preposition combination, and "management" (a collective noun) correctly takes a singular verb "acceded".

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs in SSC exams: "call off" (cancel), "call out" (summon/shout), "call on" (visit/request), "call for" (require/demand), "call up" (telephone/recall to memory).

• "Accede to" means to agree to a request/demand; do not confuse with "exceed" (to go beyond a limit).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
She / did not watched / Frankenstein / last night.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. did not watched.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "did not watched" is grammatically incorrect. In the Simple Past Tense negative, the auxiliary "did" must be followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, not the past form (V2).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense (Negative): Subject + did not + V1 + Object.

• The correct form is: "She did not watch Frankenstein last night."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Frankenstein" is correctly used as the object (a proper noun, the title of the film/novel); no error here.

• Option 3: "She" is a correctly used subject pronoun; no error here.

• Option 4: "last night." is a correctly placed time adverbial indicating the past; no error here.

NOTE

• Once "did" (the past auxiliary) appears in a sentence, the main verb always reverts to its base form (V1) — this applies in negatives ("did not go", not "did not went") and in questions ("Did she go?", not "Did she went?").

• Similarly, with "does"/"do" as auxiliaries, the main verb stays in base form: "He does not play" (not "does not plays").

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
A company can / make money by / obtain resources / more affordably.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. obtain resources.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "obtain resources" contains a grammatical error. When a verb follows a preposition (here, "by"), it must take the gerund (-ing) form, not the base form.

• Rule — Verb after a preposition: Preposition + V-ing (Gerund). Since "by" is a preposition, the verb following it must be "obtaining", not "obtain".

• The correct sentence is: "A company can make money by obtaining resources more affordably."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A company can" is correct; "can" is a modal verb correctly followed by the base verb "make" in the next segment.

• Option 2: "make money by" is correct; "by" is the appropriate preposition to indicate the means/method.

• Option 4: "more affordably." is correctly used; "affordably" is an adverb correctly modifying the manner in which resources are obtained.

NOTE

• Any verb immediately following a preposition (by, for, of, in, without, after, before, etc.) must be in the gerund (-ing) form: "He is good at singing", "She left without saying goodbye".

• Do not confuse this with verbs following modals (can, could, may, might, shall, will, must), which always take the base form: "She can sing" (not "singing").

question:
Select the option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Mahima is as smarter as Shilpi.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as smart as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the Positive Degree of comparison in the pattern "as...as", which requires the base/positive form of the adjective, not the comparative form.

• Rule — Positive Degree Comparison: as + adjective (positive/base form) + as. It is incorrect to use a comparative form (smarter) or superlative form (smartest) inside an "as...as" construction.

• The correct sentence is: "Mahima is as smart as Shilpi."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "more smart as" is incorrect; it wrongly mixes a comparative form ("more smart") with the positive-degree structure "as...as".

• Option 3: "most smart as" is incorrect; it wrongly uses a superlative form ("most smart") in a positive-degree "as...as" structure meant to compare only two people.

• Option 4: "smartest than" is incorrect on two counts: "smartest" is a superlative form (used for three or more), and superlatives are never followed by "than" — "than" is used only with comparatives (e.g., "smarter than").

NOTE

• Degrees of comparison: Positive (as...as / not so...as), Comparative (adjective + er...than / more...than, used for two), Superlative (the + adjective + est / the most...., used for three or more).

• Common SSC trap: mixing degrees, e.g., "more better", "most best", "as taller as" — all incorrect.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Conversation is indeed the (1)____________ teachable of all arts. All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a (2)_________ that interests you and your listeners. But the important thing is that you must talk about the other (3)____________ hobby rather than your own. Therein lies the secret of your (4)______________. Talk to your friends about the things that interest them, and you will get a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind. There is nothing that (5)________ people so much as your interest in their interest.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. most easily.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a superlative form, because the sentence compares conversation with "all arts" — that is, with three or more things — using the definite article "the" before the blank.

• Rule — Superlative Degree: When comparing one thing with all others in a group (three or more), the superlative form ("most" + adverb, or the -est form) is used, usually preceded by "the".

• The complete sentence reads: "Conversation is indeed the most easily teachable of all arts," meaning conversation is easier to teach/learn than any other art.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "more easily" is incorrect; "more" is a comparative form, used to compare only two things, but here conversation is being compared with "all arts" (more than two).

• Option 2: "more likely" is incorrect in meaning as well as degree; "likely" does not fit the sense of ease of teaching, and it is also comparative, not superlative.

• Option 4: "most occasionally" is incorrect; "occasionally" means "sometimes/not often" and does not fit the meaning of "easy to teach".

NOTE

• Watch for the phrase "of all" in a sentence — it is a strong signal that the superlative degree ("most", "-est") is required, not the comparative degree ("more", "-er").

• Common superlative markers: "the best", "the most important", "the largest", "the most easily".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Conversation is indeed the (1)____________ teachable of all arts. All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a (2)_________ that interests you and your listeners. But the important thing is that you must talk about the other (3)____________ hobby rather than your own. Therein lies the secret of your (4)______________. Talk to your friends about the things that interest them, and you will get a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind. There is nothing that (5)________ people so much as your interest in their interest.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. subject.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a word meaning a topic of conversation, since the sentence talks about finding something "that interests you and your listeners" to talk about.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the correct word must fit both the grammatical slot (a singular countable noun after the article "a") and the meaning of the sentence (a topic for conversation).

• The complete sentence reads: "All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a subject that interests you and your listeners," meaning you must find a topic of common interest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "credit" does not fit the meaning; "credit" refers to recognition or trust, not a topic of conversation.

• Option 3: "luxury" does not fit; "luxury" refers to comfort/indulgence, unrelated to finding a topic to talk about.

• Option 4: "result" does not fit; "result" means an outcome or consequence, not something one can "find that interests" listeners as a talking point.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (and often the surrounding sentences) before choosing an option — the correct word must fit both grammar and overall meaning/context of the passage.

• "Subject" here means "topic/theme", a common usage distinct from its other meanings (a school subject, a citizen of a country, a person undergoing treatment/experiment).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Conversation is indeed the (1)____________ teachable of all arts. All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a (2)_________ that interests you and your listeners. But the important thing is that you must talk about the other (3)____________ hobby rather than your own. Therein lies the secret of your (4)______________. Talk to your friends about the things that interest them, and you will get a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind. There is nothing that (5)________ people so much as your interest in their interest.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fellow's.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a possessive noun that can meaningfully modify "hobby", since the sentence contrasts talking about "the other ___ hobby" with "your own [hobby]".

• Rule — Possessive apostrophe: to show that something belongs to a person, add 's to a singular noun (e.g., fellow's, worker's). Here, "fellow" means a companion/other person, and "the other fellow's hobby" means "the other person's hobby".

• The complete sentence reads: "You must talk about the other fellow's hobby rather than your own," meaning you should discuss the listener's interest, not your own.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "worker's" does not fit the context; the passage is about conversation and listeners in general, not specifically about workers/employees.

• Option 2: "self's" is grammatically wrong; "self" is not normally used with a possessive apostrophe in this way, and it also contradicts the sense of the sentence, which contrasts "the other" person with "your own" self.

• Option 3: "victim's" does not fit the context; there is no mention of a victim anywhere in the passage, and it does not logically pair with "hobby" here.

NOTE

• "Fellow" (as used here) means "a companion, an associate, or another person" — as in "fellow citizen", "fellow student", "fellow traveller".

• Possessive 's is added to a singular noun to show ownership; for plural nouns ending in -s, only an apostrophe is added (e.g., "workers' demands").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Conversation is indeed the (1)____________ teachable of all arts. All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a (2)_________ that interests you and your listeners. But the important thing is that you must talk about the other (3)____________ hobby rather than your own. Therein lies the secret of your (4)______________. Talk to your friends about the things that interest them, and you will get a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind. There is nothing that (5)________ people so much as your interest in their interest.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. popularity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun that logically follows from talking to friends about things that interest them and earning "a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind" — that is, becoming well-liked.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the chosen word must complete the idea that showing interest in others' interests is the "secret" behind becoming well-liked/popular, which the rest of the sentence (about reputation and fellowship) supports.

• The complete sentence reads: "Therein lies the secret of your popularity," meaning showing genuine interest in others is the key to being liked by them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "audacity" means boldness or daring; it does not fit the context of gaining a good reputation through friendly conversation.

• Option 3: "irrationality" means a lack of logical thinking; it is unrelated to the idea of becoming well-liked through conversation.

• Option 4: "capacity" means ability or capability; while grammatically plausible, it does not carry the specific sense of "being liked/well-regarded" that the passage builds towards with "reputation for good fellowship".

NOTE

• "Popularity" means the state of being liked, admired, or supported by many people — a common theme in passages about social skills and relationships.

• Related words: popular (adjective), popularize (verb), popularly (adverb).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.
Conversation is indeed the (1)____________ teachable of all arts. All you need to do in order to become a good conversationalist is to find a (2)_________ that interests you and your listeners. But the important thing is that you must talk about the other (3)____________ hobby rather than your own. Therein lies the secret of your (4)______________. Talk to your friends about the things that interest them, and you will get a reputation for good fellowship, charming wit, and a brilliant mind. There is nothing that (5)________ people so much as your interest in their interest.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. pleases.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb meaning "to make someone happy/satisfied", since the sentence explains that showing interest in others' interests is the most effective way to make people happy.

• Rule — Subject-verb agreement: the subject of the blank verb is "nothing" (singular), so the verb must be in the singular present-tense form ending in -s: "pleases".

• The complete sentence reads: "There is nothing that pleases people so much as your interest in their interest," meaning nothing makes people happier than showing genuine interest in what interests them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "accompanies" means to go along with; it does not fit the sense of making someone happy/satisfied.

• Option 2: "admits" means to allow entry or to confess; it is unrelated to the sense of pleasing someone.

• Option 4: "advances" means to move forward or promote; it does not fit the meaning of the sentence, which is about pleasing people.

NOTE

• "Please" (verb) means to give satisfaction or happiness to someone; do not confuse with "please" used as a polite request word.

• The construction "nothing... so much as" is a common comparative idiom meaning "X is the thing that does this the most" — e.g., "Nothing pleases her so much as praise."

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The girl tried to alleviate her brother's problem.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. reduce.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "alleviate" means to make (pain, suffering, or a problem) less severe or more bearable; to lessen or reduce. (कम करना/घटाना)
◦ Example: The new medicine helped alleviate her pain considerably.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "reduce", which also means to make something smaller or less in degree.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "increase" means to make something greater in size or amount — this is the opposite of "alleviate".

• Option 2: "soar" means to rise rapidly or fly high — unrelated in meaning to "alleviate".

• Option 4: "worsen" means to make something worse — this is also opposite in meaning to "alleviate".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "alleviate": mitigate, relieve, ease, lessen, assuage.

• Antonym of "alleviate": aggravate, worsen, intensify, exacerbate.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The encounter made the audience squirm.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Relax.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "squirm" means to wriggle or twist the body due to discomfort, embarrassment, or nervousness; to feel or show acute discomfort or unease. (बेचैनी से छटपटाना)
◦ Example: He squirmed in his seat during the awkward interview.

• Its antonym among the given options is "Relax", which means to become free of tension and anxiety, i.e., to feel at ease — the opposite of feeling uncomfortable/uneasy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Speak" means to talk or say something — unrelated in meaning to "squirm" or its opposite.

• Option 3: "Chat" means to talk in a friendly, informal way — unrelated to the sense of comfort/discomfort conveyed by "squirm".

• Option 4: "Pray" means to make a request to God or a spiritual being — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "squirm": wriggle, writhe, fidget, wince.

• Other words expressing discomfort/unease often tested by SSC: "cringe", "flinch", "wince", "fidget" — their antonyms typically include "relax", "compose (oneself)", "calm".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.
The small size of his store makes it impossible for him to stock all the items.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No substitution required.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "makes it impossible" is already grammatically correct as it stands in the sentence.

• Rule — Subject-verb agreement and tense: The subject "The small size" is singular and the sentence is in the Simple Present Tense, describing a general/current fact, so the singular present-tense verb "makes" correctly agrees with it. The structure "makes it + adjective + for + object + to + infinitive" ("makes it impossible for him to stock") is a standard and correct English construction.

• Since no grammatical error exists in the original sentence, it requires no substitution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "made them impossible" is incorrect; it wrongly shifts the tense to past ("made") and wrongly changes the pronoun "it" to the plural "them", which does not agree with the singular sense required here.

• Option 2: "making it impossible" is incorrect; using the bare gerund "making" without an auxiliary verb (like "is") would leave the sentence without a finite main verb, making it grammatically incomplete.

• Option 3: "is made it impossible" is incorrect; it wrongly combines a passive-style auxiliary "is made" with the object pronoun "it" and the adjective "impossible" in a way that is not standard/grammatical English.

NOTE

• In "No substitution required" type questions, always first check whether the original underlined portion is already correct before evaluating the alternatives — SSC frequently includes one such question in every set to test this skill.

• The pattern "make/makes it + adjective + for + someone + to + verb" (e.g., "makes it difficult for her to concentrate") is a common and correct SSC-tested construction.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I would like to reach the ________ of the Everest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. peak.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "peak" means the pointed top of a mountain; the highest point. Since the sentence talks about "reaching" the highest point "of the Everest" (a mountain), "peak" is the correct word.
◦ Example: Only a few climbers manage to reach the peak of Mount Everest every year.

• The other three options are homophones or near-homophones of "peak" but carry entirely different meanings, so they do not fit the context of a mountain's summit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "peek" means to take a quick, often secretive, look at something — it does not mean "summit" and does not fit the context.

• Option 2: "pick" means to choose or select, or to remove something with fingers/a tool — unrelated to the top of a mountain.

• Option 3: "pike" refers to a type of long spear, or a type of fish, or a turnpike/road — unrelated to the top of a mountain.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones tested by SSC: peak/peek/pique (to pique one's interest), pick/pique, pique/peak.

• "Pique" (verb) means to stimulate interest or curiosity, or to feel irritated — often confused with "peak" and "peek" in spelling-based questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
John is very generous; he regularly gives alms to the poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. kind.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "generous" means showing a readiness to give more of something, especially money, than is strictly necessary or expected; kind and giving in nature. (उदार/दयालु)
◦ Example: She is generous with her time and always helps those in need.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "kind", which also conveys a caring, giving, and warm-hearted nature, consistent with John "regularly giving alms to the poor".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "popular" means well-liked by many people — this does not necessarily imply giving or kindness.

• Option 2: "great" means very good, important, or large in degree — it is too general and does not specifically capture the sense of giving/kindness.

• Option 4: "shrewd" means having sharp powers of judgement, especially in practical or business matters — this is actually closer to being clever/calculating, which is unrelated (and almost contrary) to being generous.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "generous": charitable, magnanimous, benevolent, liberal, big-hearted.

• Antonyms of "generous": stingy, miserly, selfish, greedy, tight-fisted.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Bill Gates' fortune was bequeathed for the old age home.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. to the old age home.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "bequeath" (to leave property/money to someone through a will) is conventionally followed by the preposition "to", not "for".

• Rule — Verb-preposition collocation: bequeath + something + to + someone/something (the beneficiary). This mirrors similar verbs of giving, such as "give (something) to (someone)" and "donate (something) to (someone)".

• The correct sentence is: "Bill Gates' fortune was bequeathed to the old age home."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "into the old age home" is incorrect; "into" indicates movement inside a physical space, which does not fit the abstract sense of leaving money/property to a beneficiary.

• Option 3: "by the old age home" is incorrect; "by" would wrongly suggest the old age home is the agent/doer of the bequeathing, whereas it is actually the recipient.

• Option 4: "with the old age home" is incorrect; "with" does not fit the required sense of a recipient of a bequest.

NOTE

• Other verbs that take the preposition "to" when indicating a recipient: give (to), donate (to), grant (to), award (to), hand over (to).

• Do not confuse "bequeath" (to leave by will) with "bestow" (to present as an honour or gift), which is also followed by "on/upon" (e.g., "bestow an honour upon someone").

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The coach was optimistic that Ronald will play the quarter final.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Doubtful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "optimistic" means hopeful and confident about the future or the success of something. (आशावादी)
◦ Example: She remained optimistic about her chances of winning the match.

• Its antonym among the given options is "Doubtful", which means feeling uncertain or lacking confidence about something — the opposite of feeling hopeful/confident.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Tasteful" means having or showing good aesthetic judgement — unrelated in meaning to "optimistic".

• Option 2: "Cheerful" means noticeably happy and positive — this is actually close in meaning to "optimistic", not opposite.

• Option 4: "Helpful" means giving assistance or being useful — unrelated in meaning to "optimistic".

NOTE

• The most direct antonym of "optimistic" is "pessimistic" (expecting the worst); when it is not among the options, the closest available word conveying uncertainty/lack of hope — such as "doubtful" — is chosen.

• Other synonyms of "optimistic": hopeful, positive, confident, upbeat.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to correct the sentence by using the proper meaning of the underlined word.
He scores good marks in exams as he is quite meticulous.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Careful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "meticulous" means showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise. (सावधान/चौकस)
◦ Example: The scientist was meticulous in recording every observation during the experiment.

• Since the sentence says he scores good marks "as he is quite meticulous", the word that best fits this cause-effect relationship is "Careful", which correctly conveys the sense of "meticulous".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Selective" means carefully choosing only what is thought best/appropriate — this is a different quality from being detail-oriented/careful in one's work.

• Option 3: "Intelligent" means having a high mental capacity or being clever — this describes innate ability, not the attention-to-detail trait meant by "meticulous".

• Option 4: "Lazy" means unwilling to work or use effort — this is nearly opposite in meaning to "meticulous" and does not fit the positive cause given in the sentence.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "meticulous": thorough, precise, painstaking, scrupulous, fastidious.

• Antonym of "meticulous": careless, sloppy, negligent, haphazard.

question:
Choose an appropriate word that can substitute the bracketed word and complete the sentence meaningfully.
He never (talks) the truth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. speaks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct collocation is "speak the truth", meaning to say what is factually correct or honest. (सच बोलना)
◦ Example: A person of integrity always speaks the truth, even when it is difficult.

• The word "talks" does not collocate naturally with "the truth" in standard English; the standard expression uses "speaks" (or "tells") the truth, not "talks" the truth.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "declares" means to state something officially or emphatically — "declares the truth" is not the natural, idiomatic collocation used in everyday English.

• Option 3: "narrates" means to tell a story or give an account of events in detail — it does not collocate naturally with "the truth" in this simple, general sense.

• Option 4: "utters" means to make a sound or say something (often used for a word/sound rather than an abstract concept like "the truth"); "utters the truth" is not the standard idiomatic collocation.

NOTE

• Standard collocations with "truth": speak the truth, tell the truth, admit the truth, hide the truth, distort the truth.

• Similarly, "tell a lie" (not "speak a lie") is the standard collocation — collocations often do not follow a single fixed pattern and must be memorised.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Professor Singh is not in the office today. I ask you try call him tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. suggest you try calling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "ask you try call" is grammatically faulty; it lacks the correct verb pattern and tense sense required by the context.

• Rule — Verb + object + to-infinitive / gerund patterns: The verb "suggest" fits the context of offering advice about a future action ("I suggest you try calling him tomorrow"). Additionally, "try" in the sense of "making an attempt" is idiomatically followed by a gerund (try + V-ing) — "try calling" — when suggesting an experimental action to see if it works.

• The correct sentence is: "Professor Singh is not in the office today. I suggest you try calling him tomorrow."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "am suggesting you calling" is incorrect; the Present Continuous Tense ("am suggesting") is not appropriate here, as this is a general suggestion, not an action happening at this very moment; also "suggesting you calling" is not a correct verb pattern.

• Option 3: "ask you to try called" is incorrect; after "try to", a base verb is required, not the past form "called" — the correct pattern would be "try to call" or "try calling", never "try called".

• Option 4: "asked you to call" is incorrect; the past tense "asked" does not fit the context, which refers to a suggestion for tomorrow (future), not something already asked in the past.

NOTE

• "Try + to + V1" means to make an effort to do something (may or may not succeed), while "try + V-ing" means to experiment with an action to see if it produces the desired result — both are correct, but the sense differs slightly; "try calling him" fits naturally here.

• "Suggest" is typically followed by "that + subject + base verb" (suggest that he call) or simply "subject + base verb/V-ing" in informal usage — never by "to + infinitive" (incorrect: "suggest you to call").

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
When the famous businessman / faced a huge loss / in his business, / no one expressed simpathy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. no one expressed simpathy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "simpathy" is spelt incorrectly in this segment; the correct spelling is "sympathy".

• Spelling key: SYM + PATHY. The prefix is "sym-" (meaning "together/with", from Greek), not "sim-"; it combines with "-pathy" (feeling), from Greek "sympatheia".

• The correctly spelt sentence reads: "...no one expressed sympathy."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in his business," — correctly spelt; no error here.

• Option 2: "When the famous businessman" — correctly spelt; no error here.

• Option 4: "faced a huge loss" — correctly spelt; no error here.

NOTE

• Other words with the Greek prefix "sym-"/"syn-" (together/with): symphony, symbol, symmetry, synonym, synthesis, syndrome.

• Commonly misspelt words related to feelings, often tested by SSC: sympathy, empathy, apathy — all sharing the Greek root "-pathy" (feeling/suffering).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A wild goose chase
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Fruitless search.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a wild goose chase" means a foolish and hopeless search for or pursuit of something that is unattainable or does not exist; a fruitless search. (व्यर्थ की खोज)
◦ Example: The police were sent on a wild goose chase after a false tip-off.

• The idiom originates from a 16th-century horse race in which riders had to follow a lead rider in an erratic pattern resembling the disorderly flight formation of wild geese — a pursuit that led nowhere in particular.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Ideal seeking" does not match the meaning of the idiom; there is no established idiom or meaning connecting "wild goose chase" to seeking an ideal.

• Option 3: "Fruitful search" is the near-opposite of the correct meaning; "a wild goose chase" specifically implies a search that yields nothing, not one that succeeds.

• Option 4: "On a hunt" is too literal and vague; it misses the essential sense of futility/uselessness carried by the idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms of futility/fruitlessness often tested by SSC: "a fool's errand" (a pointless task), "to flog a dead horse" (to waste effort on something already settled), "a storm in a teacup" (a lot of fuss over nothing).

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
The ministir ordered the engineers to build roads through high mountains and bridges across deep ravines in a week.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ministir.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Ministir" is spelt incorrectly; the correct spelling is "Minister" — a person appointed to head a government department.

• Spelling key: MIN + IS + TER. The word ends in "-ister", not "-istir"; it derives from the Latin "minister", meaning "servant/attendant".

• The correctly spelt sentence reads: "The Minister ordered the engineers to build roads..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Ravines" — correctly spelt; means deep, narrow gorges.

• Option 2: "Engineers" — correctly spelt; note the sequence "gi" followed by "neers".

• Option 4: "Bridges" — correctly spelt; plural of "bridge".

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt "-ister/-aster" ending words tested by SSC: sinister, canister, register, disaster, administer.

• Do not confuse "Minister" (a government official) with "Minster" (a large or important church, e.g., York Minster).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank.
The meeting was brought to a ________ (rapid) conclusion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. hasty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "rapid" means happening or moving quickly; swift. (तेज़/शीघ्र)
◦ Example: The negotiations came to a rapid end once both sides agreed.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "hasty", which also means done with excessive speed or urgency — fitting the sense of a meeting ending "quickly".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "stubborn" means refusing to change one's mind or position — unrelated in meaning to "rapid/quick".

• Option 2: "pervious" means permeable, allowing liquid to pass through — completely unrelated in meaning to "rapid".

• Option 3: "grim" means unpleasant, harsh, or serious in appearance — unrelated in meaning to "rapid/quick".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "rapid": swift, quick, speedy, brisk, prompt.

• "Hasty" can also carry a slightly negative connotation (done too quickly, without enough thought), as in "a hasty decision" — useful to note for other vocabulary-based SSC questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
An old head on young shoulders
option_1: A young person who looks old.
option_2: A young person who is lazy.
option_3: A person who is slow at understanding things.
option_4: A young person who acts or speaks like an older person.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A young person who acts or speaks like an older person.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "an old head on young shoulders" is used to describe a young person who is unusually wise, mature, or sensible for their age — someone who thinks and behaves like someone much older. (कम उम्र में समझदार)
◦ Example: Despite being only sixteen, she has an old head on young shoulders and manages her finances very sensibly.

• The idiom contrasts "an old head" (wisdom/maturity, associated with age) with "young shoulders" (youth), to praise unusual maturity in a young person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A young person who looks old." describes physical appearance, not wisdom or maturity, which is the actual sense of the idiom.

• Option 2: "A young person who is lazy." is unrelated to the idiom; laziness is not implied at all.

• Option 3: "A person who is slow at understanding things." is nearly opposite in meaning; the idiom actually praises sharp understanding and maturity, not slowness.

NOTE

• Other idioms about wisdom/maturity often tested by SSC: "wise beyond one's years" (similar meaning to this idiom), "a chip off the old block" (a child who resembles a parent in character).

• Contrast with idioms about immaturity: "green horn" (an inexperienced person), "wet behind the ears" (young and inexperienced).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The poet was lost in a reverie.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Reality.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "reverie" means a state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts; a daydream. (दिवास्वप्न/ख़याली दुनिया में खोए रहना)
◦ Example: She was lost in a reverie about her childhood home.

• Its antonym among the given options is "Reality", which refers to the actual state of things as they truly exist, as opposed to imagination or daydreaming — the direct opposite of "reverie".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Fantasy" is close in meaning to "reverie" (an imaginative daydream), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Daydream" is essentially a synonym of "reverie", not its antonym.

• Option 4: "Trance" is also close in meaning to "reverie" (a dreamlike, half-conscious state), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "reverie": daydream, musing, trance, fantasy, woolgathering.

• Antonym pairs frequently tested by SSC around states of mind: reverie/reality, illusion/fact, fantasy/actuality.
